title: Laboratory Automation and Simulation
answer: Self-driving labs, digital twins, instrument data, protocol optimisation and supply forecasting.

children.name: Self-Driving Laboratories
children.blurb: Self-driving laboratories combine robotic hardware, automated instruments, and machine learning to plan and run experiments with limited human intervention.

children.name: Digital Twins for Experiments
children.blurb: Digital twins for experiments are computational models that mirror a physical experimental system, its instruments, samples, and protocols, so that a planned procedure can be simulated before it is run on real equipment.

children.name: Instrument and Sensor Data
children.blurb: Instrument and sensor data in laboratory automation covers the readings produced by analytical instruments, environmental monitors, robotic systems, and embedded sensors during experiments and routine operations.

children.name: Optimising Lab Protocols
children.blurb: Optimising lab protocols covers the use of AI and simulation to improve experimental procedures in laboratory settings, including reagent volumes, timing, temperature, and the order of steps.

children.name: Forecasting Lab Supplies
children.blurb: Forecasting lab supplies means estimating future consumption of reagents, consumables, glassware, and replacement parts across a laboratory or network of labs.

sections.body: Laboratory automation and simulation is the use of artificial intelligence to run physical experiments, model them before they happen, and manage the data and materials around them. In practice this means robotic platforms that choose and perform their own next experiment, software that builds a working copy of an instrument or process, and systems that read raw sensor output to spot drift or failure. It also covers the less glamorous work of tuning a protocol, such as reagent volumes or temperature steps, and predicting how much of each supply a lab will need next month. These are not futuristic ideas, they are working systems in chemistry, materials science, and biology labs today.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The honest state of the field is uneven. Self-driving laboratories work well for narrow, well-defined search spaces, like finding a better catalyst or a formulation, but they still struggle with tasks that require human judgement about what is worth trying. Digital twins are reliable for simple instruments and predictable processes, yet a full twin of a complex biological system remains out of reach. Instrument data cleaning and anomaly detection are fairly mature, while protocol optimisation often works only when the search space is small and the assay is fast. Supply forecasting is useful for stable, high-volume consumables but breaks down when suppliers change or a new project starts. The limits are real: many published results come from a single lab or a single instrument, and generalisation across sites is still an open problem.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with Self-Driving Laboratories to see the overall loop of planning, running, and learning from experiments, since the other pages feed into that loop. Digital Twins for Experiments explains the simulated counterpart that lets a lab test changes without wasting materials, and it pairs naturally with Instrument and Sensor Data, which covers the raw measurements that make a twin accurate. Optimising Lab Protocols is the page for someone who already has a working assay and wants to make it faster, cheaper, or more reproducible, while Forecasting Lab Supplies addresses the operational side of keeping a lab running. Together these five pages draw on the site's library of 135 research papers and 10,555 extracted claims, so each page links back to the original studies rather than to a secondary search tool.
